strengths: Addresses a relevant navigation problem: associating locally perceived HD lane geometry with global SD road networks. The benchmark could support useful research beyond standalone online map reconstruction.
Includes both ground-truth and predicted HD maps, with geographically separated PON splits and MapTRv2 retraining described in the appendix.
Reports substantial improvements over HMM: 42.3 versus 36.0 association F1 on OMA and 78.7 versus 70.1 association precision on OMA-GT.
Provides component ablations, model-size comparisons, and qualitative failure cases. Combining path-aware and spatial attention clearly improves over either component alone.
weaknesses: Comparisons are insufficient to establish competitiveness. Only KNN and HMM are evaluated; there are no learned graph-matching, generic transformer, or stronger geometric/topological alignment baselines. Much of MAT adapts existing attention, serialization, and positional-encoding techniques, so its methodological contribution requires stronger comparisons.

The central evaluation metric is insufficiently specified. Algorithm 1 leaves point/path matching, sequence consistency, overlap calculation, and length-bin aggregation largely undefined. Its treatment of association errors as false positives without clearly corresponding false negatives makes recall difficult to interpret; identical HD geometry does not itself guarantee correct association recall. Equation 8 also sums threshold scores without the normalization required by the claimed mean.

The decoding formulation has a concrete defect: Equation 15 maximizes cumulative log probability over all intermediate beam lengths, including the initial seed. Since added log probabilities are nonpositive, this favors the seed over completed paths. The equations also omit the advertised connectivity restriction and introduce conditional probabilities and an end token not defined by the association head.

Other implementation details remain unresolved. CTC is described as aligning feature sequences without specifying discrete targets or blank handling. Enumerating all root-to-leaf paths requires an explicit policy for cycles, combinatorial growth, and conflicting predictions on shared segments.

Benchmark quality is not adequately audited. Labels originate from MAT trained on proprietary data, but manual correction rates and independent annotation accuracy are unreported. OMA excludes low-quality predictions without defining the filtering criterion, potentially biasing evaluation. Only one perception model is tested, and all component ablations use OMA-GT.

Navigation and robustness claims exceed the evidence. There is no downstream planning or route-success evaluation, controlled GPS-shift study, or systematic missing-lane/noise experiment. The predicted-map results alone do not establish dependable navigation.

Reproducibility is weakened by contradictory reporting. The main text, Table 9, and Appendix F.2 give different learning rates and training settings. The conclusion reports OMA F1 as 32.3, whereas Table 1 reports 42.3. Small ablation gains of 0.1–0.3 points lack repeated-run uncertainty estimates.

Efficiency comparisons use an A6000 GPU for MAT and explicitly unoptimized CPU Python/NumPy implementations for KNN/HMM. These measurements do not substantiate the claimed efficiency advantage or Pareto frontier, and association latency excludes online map construction.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: associating local HD lane geometry with global SD road networks to support navigation. The distinction between association using ground-truth maps (OMA-GT) and predicted maps (OMA) is useful.
MAT shows meaningful reported improvements over the implemented baselines: OMA association F1 increases from 36.0 for HMM to 42.3, and OMA-GT association precision increases from 70.1 to 78.7.

The paper includes component ablations, model-size comparisons, qualitative failures, and supplementary implementation details. The reported use of the geographically separated PON split and retraining of MapTRv2 are positive evaluation choices.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish competitiveness against strong alternatives. Only KNN and HMM are evaluated; there are no learned graph-matching, generic transformer, or geometry-plus-topology baselines. MAT largely combines established attention, serialization, positional encoding, and decoding techniques, so stronger comparisons are necessary to establish its methodological contribution.

The central evaluation metric is insufficiently specified and internally inconsistent. Algorithm 1 leaves point matching, path matching, sequence consistency, and overlap calculations abstract, and does not explicitly account for unmatched predicted paths as false positives. Equation 8 sums threshold-specific precision and recall rather than averaging them as the text states. The claim that recall becomes irrelevant on OMA-GT also needs justification: identical geometry does not guarantee correct association labels. These issues prevent reliable independent reproduction of the benchmark.

Dataset quality claims lack quantitative validation. Initial annotations come from MAT trained on proprietary data, followed by manual refinement, but no independent annotation audit, inter-annotator agreement, or residual error rate is reported. This leaves possible model-specific annotation bias unmeasured. Appendix A also excludes low-quality MapTRv2 predictions without specifying the filtering criteria or evaluating the excluded cases, potentially selecting away important deployment failures.

Navigation and robustness claims exceed the evidence. There is no downstream route-following or planning evaluation, no controlled GPS-shift or missing-lane stress test, and no evaluation with another online map predictor. All component ablations use OMA-GT, so their benefits under the noisy conditions motivating OMA remain unverified. Small gains of 0.1–0.3 points are reported without seed variability or confidence intervals.

Several method details remain unresolved. CTC is described as aligning feature sequences without specifying the discrete targets, blank symbol, or repeated-label handling. Enumerating all root-to-leaf paths requires clarification for cyclic road graphs and potentially combinatorial path counts. In Appendix E.3, Equation 15 maximizes unnormalized cumulative log-probability over beams from every length; as written, the initial singleton cannot be improved by adding nonpositive log-probabilities. The actual completed-path decoding rule therefore needs correction.

Efficiency comparisons are not controlled: MAT runs on an A6000 GPU, whereas KNN and HMM use explicitly unoptimized Python/NumPy implementations on a CPU. These measurements do not substantiate algorithmic speed advantages. Moreover, accepting latency because nuScenes annotations are sampled at 2 Hz does not establish suitability for a deployed navigation stack, and end-to-end perception-plus-association latency is not reported.

Reproducibility is weakened by substantial contradictions. Section 6.1 specifies learning rate 1e-4, weight decay 0.05, batch size 128, and one warm-up epoch; Table 9 gives different learning rate, weight decay, and warm-up settings; Appendix F.2 instead states learning rate 2e-3 and batch size 12. The conclusion reports OMA F1 of 32.3 rather than Table 1's 42.3. The submitted abstract also supplies no usable code or dataset link despite announcing one. Together, these problems leave the benchmark and empirical findings insufficiently reliable for acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: associating local lane-level HD maps with global road-level SD maps to support navigation. The task formulation and proposed benchmark could be useful contributions.

Evaluating both ground-truth HD maps (OMA-GT) and predicted maps (OMA) usefully distinguishes association performance from perception-related degradation. The stated use of the geographically separated PON split is a positive design choice.
MAT reports substantial improvements over the evaluated baselines: 42.3 versus 36.0 association F1 on OMA and 78.7 versus 70.1 association precision on OMA-GT compared with HMM.

The ablations support combining path-aware and spatial attention: their combination achieves 77.8 precision versus 74.1 and 62.1 individually. Model-size experiments and qualitative failure cases provide additional useful analysis.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not establish competitiveness against strong learned alternatives. Only KNN and HMM are evaluated externally; generic transformers, graph neural networks, and adapted graph-matching methods are missing. Given the reuse of serialized attention from Point Transformer V3 and established positional encodings, stronger comparisons are necessary to establish the architectural contribution.

The benchmark metric is insufficiently specified for a central contribution. Algorithm 1 leaves point/path matching, sequence consistency, overlap calculation, and treatment of unmatched predicted paths largely abstract. Equation 8 sums threshold scores rather than averaging them, contrary to the prose. The justification for omitting association recall on OMA-GT also conflates perfect geometric correspondence with correct road-label association.

Dataset quality and construction need stronger evidence. Labels originate from MAT trained on proprietary maps, but manual verification coverage, independent annotation agreement, and residual error rates are not reported. Appendix A excludes low-quality predicted maps without specifying the selection rule, potentially biasing the evaluation. The headline 30K+ dataset description also obscures that predicted-map OMA contains only 5,573 test samples.

Important method details remain unresolved. CTC is described as aligning feature sequences without specifying discrete targets or blank handling. Root-to-leaf path enumeration does not explain cycles or control of combinatorial growth. More seriously, Equation 15 selects the highest cumulative log-probability across all partial sequence lengths, including the initial seed; because extensions add nonpositive terms, this favors the seed rather than a completed association. The stated connectivity constraints are also absent from the appendix's candidate-set equation.

The evaluation does not substantiate the broader navigation and robustness claims. There is no downstream planning or route-success experiment, controlled GPS-shift or missing-lane stress test, or evaluation with another perception model. All component ablations use OMA-GT, leaving their effectiveness under the central noisy online-map setting uncertain. Small gains from RoPE, CTC, and post-processing lack uncertainty estimates.

The efficiency comparison is not controlled: MAT runs on an A6000 GPU, whereas KNN and HMM use explicitly unoptimized Python/NumPy CPU implementations. These measurements establish MAT's reported runtime but not its computational superiority. End-to-end latency including online map construction is not reported.

Reproducibility is weakened by conflicting training configurations across Section 6.1, Table 9, and Appendix F.2, including learning rate, batch size, weight decay, and warm-up duration. The conclusion reports 32.3 OMA F1 whereas Table 1 reports 42.3. The abstract's promised code/dataset link is missing. Together with the metric and decoding ambiguities, these issues prevent confident reproduction and place the submission below the acceptance threshold despite its promising motivation.

strengths: The task is practically relevant: associating inexpensive SD maps with online lane maps addresses a useful gap between road-level routing and local perception. OMA provides substantial annotation effort and a potentially valuable benchmark.

MAT achieves consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines. MAT-T improves NR-F1 over EAM3 by 5.3 points on ground-truth maps and by 4.0–5.7 points across three perception generators, with reported association latency around 35 ms.

The evaluation includes architectural ablations, cross-city transfer, data-efficiency experiments, synthetic SD-map perturbations, and environmental corruptions. The path-aware attention ablation provides concrete evidence that topology helps.
The appendix candidly examines failures and performance degradation on complex road geometries, providing useful context beyond aggregate scores.
weaknesses: The central evaluation metric is not consistently specified. Equation 7 sums rather than averages across thresholds, while Appendix E.1 states that validation recall is always one and substitutes precision for F1. This differs from the stated harmonic-mean definition and raises questions about how semantic mismatches contribute false negatives. Algorithm 1 does not fully resolve matching multiplicities or aggregation. These issues undermine reproducibility of the principal reported results.

The path-attention complexity claim is unsupported. Appendix F.1 enumerates and duplicates tokens across all root-to-leaf paths, whose number can grow exponentially even in acyclic graphs; the asserted cubic worst case and linear average case are not justified. Handling cycles, components without roots, and path-count limits is unspecified. Runtime scaling and tail latency are needed to support the efficiency claims.

The topology-constrained decoder is not correctly formalized. Equations 10–13 expand over all roads without expressing the promised connectivity restriction, and Equation 14 maximizes cumulative log probability over partial sequences of every length. As written, extending a sequence cannot improve its score, so an initial short hypothesis can dominate completed outputs. Direction-conditioned probabilities and reconciliation of shared tokens across paths are also unexplained.

Benchmark independence and construction need stronger documentation. Validation and test reuse the same scenes and ground-truth annotations, so the test is a noisy-input evaluation rather than an independent held-out assessment. Appendix D.1 also excludes 40 low-quality predictions without specifying the exclusion rule or reporting results on the complete set. Annotation correction rates do not establish residual label accuracy, and code and annotations are only promised upon publication.

Baseline breadth does not fully establish comparison fairness or architectural novelty. The adaptations, tuning budgets, and many-to-one handling of graph/point matching baselines are insufficiently described. Spatial serialization resembles existing point-transformer designs, while the PTv3 comparison lacks enough implementation detail to isolate the proposed contribution. Most component ablations use clean maps, leaving their specific contribution to noisy-map robustness less established.

The demonstrated outcome is local association, not validated lane-level navigation. There is no route-success or downstream planning evaluation, and the reported latency excludes upstream perception. Metric sensitivity is substantial: Table 19 changes test NR-F1 from 6.6 to 72.4 by varying the geometric threshold from 0.5 to 2 m. An oracle-association ceiling and separate geometry/association measurements would clarify the bottleneck. High-complexity test paths score around 10–12 in Table 10, further limiting claims of reliable navigation.

strengths: The task is practically relevant: associating road-level SD maps with perceived lane networks could connect global navigation to local perception. OMA provides potentially valuable correspondence annotations and uses a geographical training/evaluation split.

The reported improvements are consistent across perception generators. MAT-T exceeds EAM3 by 5.2, 5.7, and 4.0 points on MapTR, MapTRv2, and SeqGrowGraph inputs, respectively, with substantially lower reported association latency.

The experiments include substantial component ablations, cross-city transfer, environmental corruptions, SD-map perturbations, and failure analysis. Table 3 provides concrete evidence that path-aware attention benefits association.
weaknesses: The central evaluation metric is inconsistently defined. Equation 7 sums rather than averages precision and recall across thresholds, contrary to the main text. Appendix E.1 additionally substitutes precision for validation F1 because recall is allegedly always one, although F1 would then equal 2P/(1+P). Whether association failures generate false negatives is unclear across the narrative and Algorithm 1. These issues prevent confident interpretation and reproduction of the headline scores.

The path-attention complexity claims are not justified. Appendix F.1 enumerates and duplicates all root-to-leaf paths, whose number can grow exponentially even in a directed acyclic graph. Its claimed polynomial worst case and linear average complexity require additional graph assumptions or explicit path limits. Handling cycles and components without roots or leaves is also unspecified.

The formal decoding algorithm does not implement the claimed constraints adequately. Equation 10 expands over all roads without expressing connectivity restrictions. Equation 14 selects among prefixes of every length using accumulated log probabilities, which favors the initial seed because extensions cannot increase the score. The relationship between the conditional probabilities in Equation 11 and the tokenwise classifier is also undefined.

The benchmark lacks an independent final holdout: validation and test reuse the same underlying scenes and annotations with different OP inputs. This supports a controlled perception-noise comparison, but does not provide an untouched test set after validation-based tuning. Appendix D.1 also excludes 40 low-quality predictions without specifying an objective exclusion rule.

The evidence establishes association improvements rather than successful lane-level navigation. There is no route-conditioned lane-selection or route-completion evaluation, and the reported latency excludes upstream perception. The robustness claims also need qualification: Table 10 reports only approximately 10–12% on several high-complexity test bins.

Baseline adaptation and methodological positioning need more detail. The paper does not sufficiently explain how one-to-one graph/point matching methods are adapted to many-to-one association or how path-based baselines are batched and tuned for timing comparisons. The relationship to Point Transformer V3 serialization is underdeveloped despite its inclusion as a baseline. Code and annotations are promised only upon publication, leaving these implementation-dependent questions unresolved.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: associating local perception maps with road-level navigation maps. OMA’s lane-to-road annotations could provide a valuable benchmark for this comparatively underexplored task.

The reported improvements are consistent across three perception generators. MAT-T exceeds EAM3 by 5.2, 5.7, and 4.0 points on MapTR, MapTRv2, and SeqGrowGraph inputs, respectively, with substantially lower reported association latency.
The ablations support combining path-aware and spatial attention: their combination achieves 77.8 versus 74.1 for path-aware attention alone and 62.1 for spatial attention alone.

The evaluation includes useful cross-city transfers, data-efficiency experiments, synthetic map perturbations, environmental corruptions, and failure analysis. Geographic separation of training and evaluation regions is also a positive design choice.
weaknesses: The central evaluation metric is internally inconsistent. Appendix E.1 sums over thresholds without normalization and substitutes precision for F1 on validation because recall is reportedly one; mathematically, F1 would instead equal 2P/(1+P). Moreover, semantic mismatches should affect recall under the main text’s joint geometric-semantic definition. Algorithm 1 does not resolve this discrepancy. These issues leave the headline scores insufficiently specified and make validation/test comparisons difficult to interpret.

The efficiency analysis overlooks path enumeration. Appendix F.1 enumerates and duplicates tokens over all root-to-leaf paths, yet claims polynomial worst-case and linear average complexity without adequate assumptions. Repeated branching and merging can produce exponentially many paths, and cyclic components may have no roots or leaves. Cycle handling, path limits, and latency scaling with graph complexity are needed to substantiate the real-time claim.

The benchmark lacks a separate held-out test geography beyond the validation regions: validation and test use the same scenes with different OP representations. This is useful for controlled noise analysis, but does not establish independent test performance after model selection. Appendix D.1 also excludes 40 low-quality prediction scenarios without specifying the exclusion criterion, potentially removing difficult deployment cases.

Baseline adaptation and reproducibility are insufficiently documented. The paper does not adequately explain how graph/point matching methods are adapted to many-to-one association, how conflicting path-level predictions are reconciled, or how OP connectivity is obtained from each generator. Code and annotations are promised only upon publication. These details matter for verifying both accuracy and the large latency advantages.

The demonstrated task is association, while the broader claim is accurate lane-level navigation. There is no route-conditioned lane-selection or route-completion evaluation, and association alone does not guarantee a connected, legally traversable lane route. Requiring every predicted lane to match exactly one SD road also leaves false-positive lanes and missing SD roads without an explicit unmatched outcome.

Several results require reconciliation. The equal-bin aggregation described in Appendix E.2 does not reproduce Table 9 from Table 10: the ten listed bins average approximately 53.9/23.6 for validation/test, rather than 60.3/32.5. Performance also drops sharply on complex paths, reaching 11.6 on the highest-complexity test bin. Without baseline comparisons on these difficult cases or uncertainty estimates, the broad robustness claims remain stronger than the evidence.
